title: Sargable Date Ranges
description: YEAR()/MONTH() on a date column blocks the index; a half-open date range (>= start AND < end) seeks instead. Why it matters: date filtering ("this month", "today", "this year") appears in nearly every report -- writing it in a sargable form is a core, everyday skill.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About
This lesson extends the "sargable" idea from earlier lessons specifically to dates — a place where developers very commonly, and very innocently, break index usage without realizing it. You'll see how wrapping a date column in functions like `YEAR()` or `MONTH()` can silently disable an index built on exactly that column.

Why does this happen? Just like with arithmetic, once you apply a function to the column itself — `YEAR(OrderDate) = 2025` — SQL Server can no longer compare your filter directly against the sorted, raw values stored in the index. The index stores actual date values like `2025-06-15`, not "the year part" of each date. To check "does the year equal 2025," the database would have to compute the year for every single row first, which throws away the whole benefit of having a sorted index.

Think of a filing cabinet of documents sorted by their full date. If someone asks "find me every document filed sometime in 2025," but insists you extract just the year from each folder label one at a time to check it, you're back to checking every single folder — the sorted-by-full-date order doesn't help you skip any of them. The fix is to rewrite the condition as a plain range on the raw column instead — `WHERE OrderDate >= '2025-06-01' AND OrderDate < '2025-07-01'` — so the database can jump straight to the June 2025 section using the sort order it already has.

## Scenario
A monthly sales report runs `... WHERE YEAR(OrderDate) = 2025 AND MONTH(OrderDate) = 6` against a 200,000-row `Orders` table. There is even a covering index on `OrderDate`, yet the report still scans the whole table.

## Why it's slow
Wrapping the indexed column in a function — `YEAR(OrderDate)`, `MONTH(OrderDate)` — makes the predicate **non-sargable** (Search ARGument ABLE). SQL Server must compute `YEAR()`/`MONTH()` for *every* row before it can test it, so it cannot navigate the B-tree to the matching dates. The result is a full **Index Scan** of the covering index instead of a targeted seek.

## What to look for
- In the plan: an **Index Scan** on `IX_Orders_OrderDate` touching all 200k rows.
- In `STATISTICS IO`: hundreds of **logical reads** for a query that returns one month of data.

## The concept
Rewrite the filter as a **half-open range** — `OrderDate >= '2025-06-01' AND OrderDate < '2025-07-01'` — leaving the column bare. Now the index can **seek** straight to June 2025 and read only that slice. Half-open (`>= start AND < next-start`) is preferred over `BETWEEN` because it is correct for `datetime`/`datetime2` values with a time component.

_This query returns several thousand rows, so we grade on the plan **operator** and **logical reads**, not the row set itself._
startingQuery: SELECT OrderId, CustomerId, OrderDate, Total FROM Orders WHERE YEAR(OrderDate) = 2025 AND MONTH(OrderDate) = 6;
hints: Look at the operator reading Orders — is it an Index Scan or an Index Seek? A function around OrderDate forces a scan.
SQL Server can only seek when the indexed column appears bare on one side of the comparison.
Rewrite as a half-open range: WHERE OrderDate >= '2025-06-01' AND OrderDate < '2025-07-01'.
